lessons.title: Copy Any Clearance: CRAFT
lessons.hook: ATC talks at 200 words a minute. Here's how you win.

quiz.question: In CRAFT, what does the first C stand for?
quiz.explanation: Every IFR clearance starts with the clearance limit — usually your destination airport. (AIM 4-4-3)

quiz.question: You hear "cleared to Denver as filed." What should you still expect to copy?
quiz.explanation: "As filed" covers the route only. The A, F, and T of CRAFT — altitude, frequency, transponder — are still coming.

quiz.question: Why write C-R-A-F-T on your pad before calling clearance delivery?
choices: Clearances follow that exact order, so you just fill in blanks
ATC will ask you to read the letters back
quiz.explanation: Clearance items are issued in a standard order (AIM 4-4-3). Pre-writing CRAFT turns a fast readback into a fill-in-the-blank.

lessons.title: The 1-2-3 Rule: When You Need an Alternate
lessons.hook: Do you legally need an alternate today? Count to three.

quiz.question: Forecast at destination, ETA ±1 hr: ceiling 1,500 ft, visibility 5 SM. Alternate required?
choices: Yes — the ceiling is below 2,000 ft
quiz.explanation: You need BOTH ≥2,000 ft and ≥3 SM from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA. 1,500 ft fails, so file an alternate. (91.169)

quiz.question: Standard alternate minimums at an airport with only a VOR (non-precision) approach?
quiz.explanation: Standard alternate minimums: 600-2 precision, 800-2 non-precision, at the time of your ETA. (91.169(c))

quiz.question: Your alternate has no instrument approach at all. To list it, the weather must allow...
choices: Descent from the MEA, approach, and landing under basic VFR
quiz.explanation: With no IAP at the alternate, 91.169 requires ceilings/visibility allowing a descent from the MEA and a landing under basic VFR.

lessons.title: Holding Entries Without the Headache
lessons.hook: Cleared to hold. Which entry? You've got until the fix to decide.

quiz.question: The three standard holding entries are:
quiz.explanation: AIM 5-3-8 recommends direct, parallel, and teardrop entries based on your heading relative to the holding course.

quiz.question: The recommended entry sectors are divided by a line drawn at what angle to the inbound holding course?
quiz.explanation: The 70° line through the fix splits the non-direct region into the parallel and teardrop sectors.

quiz.question: In a teardrop entry, after crossing the fix you fly...
choices: ~30° off the outbound course on the holding side, then turn to intercept inbound
Parallel to the inbound course on the non-holding side
quiz.explanation: Teardrop: proceed on an outbound track ~30° to the holding side, then turn back to intercept the inbound course. (AIM 5-3-8)

lessons.title: Lost Comms: AVEF & MEA
lessons.hook: The radio just died in the clouds. What now?

faa.title: IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure

quiz.question: Lost comms in IMC. Route priority under 91.185 is:
quiz.explanation: AVEF: the route Assigned; if being Vectored, direct to the fix/route the vector was for; then Expected; then Filed.

quiz.question: Lost comms altitude for each segment is the HIGHEST of:
quiz.explanation: 91.185(c)(2): fly the highest of the minimum IFR altitude (MEA), the altitude ATC told you to expect, or your last assigned altitude.

quiz.question: Radio fails and you encounter VFR conditions. You should:
choices: Continue VFR and land as soon as practicable
Climb back into IMC and fly AVEF
quiz.explanation: 91.185(b): if you hit VFR conditions after the failure, remain VFR and land as soon as practicable.

lessons.title: IFR Currency: 6-6-HIT
lessons.hook: Legal to file IFR today? Let's check your math.

quiz.question: To act as PIC under IFR, within the preceding 6 calendar months you need:
choices: 6 approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting/tracking courses
6 hours of instrument time and 3 approaches
quiz.explanation: 61.57(c): six instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting/tracking courses using navigation systems.

quiz.question: Your currency lapsed 3 months ago (month 9 of 12). You may regain it by:
choices: Flying approaches with a safety pilot or in an approved sim
Filing IFR and logging 6 approaches solo in IMC
quiz.explanation: During the 6-month grace period you can regain currency yourself (safety pilot/sim/instructor) — but you can't act as PIC under IFR until you do.

quiz.question: More than 12 months since you were last instrument current. What's required?
quiz.explanation: 61.57(d): once the grace period ends, you need an IPC from an authorized instructor/examiner.

lessons.title: Brief a Plate Like a Pro
lessons.hook: Ten miles out is a terrible place to meet your approach plate.

quiz.question: A solid approach brief flows in what order?
choices: Briefing strip, notes, plan view, profile, minimums, missed
Missed approach, then plan view, then strip
Whatever order the plate prints them
quiz.explanation: Top-to-bottom keeps the brief consistent and complete — ending with minimums and the missed so they're freshest.

quiz.question: Why brief the missed approach out loud before the FAF?
choices: At minimums there's no time to read — you fly it from memory
ATC requires a readback of the missed
It's only needed for circling approaches
So your passenger can fly it
quiz.explanation: The missed happens at the busiest, lowest moment of the approach. The first steps must already be loaded in your head.

lessons.title: The ILS in Plain English
lessons.hook: Two needles, one runway, zero visibility. Meet the ILS.

quiz.question: Standard Category I ILS minimums are:
choices: DA 200 ft HAT, visibility ½ SM / RVR 1,800
quiz.explanation: A standard CAT I ILS goes down to 200 ft above touchdown with as little as ½ SM or RVR 1,800 (AIM 1-1-9; exact values are on the plate).

quiz.question: Compared to a VOR course, the localizer is:
choices: About 4x more sensitive — small corrections only
quiz.explanation: The localizer's full-scale deflection is roughly a quarter of a VOR's, so needle movements are faster — correct with small pressures.

quiz.question: Reaching DA without the runway environment in sight, you must:
choices: Level off at DA and continue to the MAP
quiz.explanation: DA is a decision altitude — no runway environment means missed approach, beginning at DA. (91.175)

lessons.title: VOR Radials Without the Vertigo
lessons.hook: Which radial are you on? Wrong answer costs you the checkride.

quiz.question: VOR radials are defined as courses...
quiz.explanation: A radial always radiates outward FROM the station — the 090 radial lies due east of the VOR.

quiz.question: You get reverse sensing on a basic CDI when:
choices: The OBS course is roughly opposite your direction of flight
You're too close to the station
quiz.explanation: With the OBS set ~180° from your actual course, the needle deflects away from the course — fly-toward-the-needle becomes wrong.

quiz.question: Why can't a properly set HSI reverse-sense?
choices: The course arrow rotates with the compass card, keeping the picture oriented to your heading
It uses GPS instead of the VOR
quiz.explanation: The HSI overlays the course needle on a heading-slaved card, so the deflection is always shown relative to where you're actually pointed.

lessons.title: LPV vs LNAV: The Minima Lines
lessons.hook: Four lines of minimums on one RNAV plate. Which one is yours?

quiz.question: Which RNAV minima line requires WAAS and provides ILS-like angular guidance?
quiz.explanation: LPV (Localizer Performance with Vertical guidance) uses WAAS for angular guidance and DAs as low as 200 ft. (AIM 1-1-18)

quiz.question: Flying to plain LNAV minimums, you descend to...
choices: An MDA — level off until the missed point or runway in sight
A DA — decide as you reach it
quiz.explanation: LNAV is lateral-only; its minimum is an MDA you must not descend below without the runway environment. (91.175)

quiz.question: Your GPS annunciates "LNAV" on an approach you briefed for LPV. You should:
choices: Ask ATC to fix your WAAS signal
quiz.explanation: The annunciated service level determines your line of minima — fly what the box is actually providing.

lessons.title: Takeoff Minimums: Legal vs Smart
lessons.hook: Zero-zero fog. Can you legally take off? ...Should you?

quiz.question: Required takeoff minimums for a Part 91 (non-commercial) flight are:
choices: None — but that doesn't make 0-0 wise
quiz.explanation: 91.175(f) applies to operators under Parts 121/125/129/135. Part 91 has no takeoff minimums — judgment is the only limit.

quiz.question: Standard takeoff minimums for a commercial operator with 2 engines:
quiz.explanation: Standard: 1 SM for aircraft with two engines or less, ½ SM for more than two. (91.175(f)(1)-(2))

quiz.question: A smart personal takeoff minimum for single-pilot IFR is weather good enough to:
choices: Return and fly an approach back into your departure airport
See the end of the runway
quiz.explanation: If trouble hits right after takeoff, your departure airport is the nearest runway — keep enough weather to use it.

lessons.title: METAR & TAF: Read Weather Like a Dispatcher
lessons.hook: KDEN 271753Z 33015G25KT... gibberish, or a go/no-go answer?

quiz.question: Which cloud reports constitute a ceiling?
quiz.explanation: A ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer, or vertical visibility into an obscuration. Scattered doesn't count.

quiz.question: In a TAF, "FM1500" means:
choices: A rapid, lasting change to new conditions beginning at 1500Z
quiz.explanation: FM (FROM) groups signal a fast, permanent change to the new conditions at that Zulu time; TEMPO covers temporary fluctuations.

quiz.question: Temperature 12°C, dew point 11°C, sun setting. Expect:
quiz.explanation: A small, closing temp/dew point spread near sunset is the classic fog setup — saturation is one degree of cooling away.

lessons.title: Icing: Where It Lives, How You Leave
lessons.hook: Ice doesn't announce itself. It just starts redesigning your wing.

faa.title: Pilot Guide: Flight in Icing Conditions

quiz.question: Structural icing requires:
choices: Visible moisture and aircraft surface temperature at or below freezing
quiz.explanation: Both ingredients are required: visible moisture (cloud, rain) and a surface at or below 0°C. (AC 91-74B)

quiz.question: Which icing type comes from large supercooled drops and forms smooth, heavy, hard-to-see accretions?
quiz.explanation: Clear ice flows back before freezing, building smooth heavy sheets — the most dangerous accretion type.

quiz.question: You encounter freezing rain. The warmer air you may need is most likely:
quiz.explanation: Freezing rain forms when precipitation falls from warmer air aloft into a below-freezing layer — a climb may reach the warm layer.

lessons.title: MEA, MOCA & Friends
lessons.hook: Five altitude acronyms guard every airway. Know who does what.

quiz.question: The MEA guarantees:
choices: Obstacle clearance AND acceptable nav signal for the whole segment
quiz.explanation: MEA covers both obstruction clearance and navigation signal coverage between fixes — that's what makes it the workhorse.

quiz.question: The MOCA assures VOR navigation signal coverage only within:
quiz.explanation: MOCA provides full obstacle clearance but signal coverage only within 22 NM of the VOR. Below the MEA, that's the catch.

quiz.question: An MCA published at a fix means you must:
choices: Cross that fix at or above the MCA
Begin your descent at that fix
Be able to receive the fix at that altitude
quiz.explanation: MCA is a crossing restriction — start the climb early so you cross at or above it (MRA is the reception altitude).

lessons.title: VOR Checks: 4-4-6-4, Every 30 Days
lessons.hook: Your VOR hasn't been checked in 31 days. Guess what's illegal now.

faa.title: VOR equipment check for IFR operations

quiz.question: Maximum bearing error for an AIRBORNE VOR checkpoint:
quiz.explanation: Airborne checkpoints allow ±6°; VOT and ground checkpoints are ±4°. (91.171)

quiz.question: Checking dual VORs against each other, the maximum permitted difference between indicated bearings is:
quiz.explanation: The dual cross-check allows a maximum of 4° between the two indicated bearings to the same station.

quiz.question: A valid VOR check log entry requires:
choices: Date, place, bearing error, and signature
quiz.explanation: 91.171(d): the person making the check logs date, place, bearing error, and signs it.

lessons.title: What You Must Tell ATC
lessons.hook: Some silence is golden. This silence is a violation.

quiz.question: Which of these must ALWAYS be reported to ATC, radar or not?
choices: Vacating a previously assigned altitude for a new one
quiz.explanation: Leaving an assigned altitude for a newly assigned one is on the always-report list. (AIM 5-3-3)

quiz.question: You must report a change in average true airspeed of:
quiz.explanation: A TAS change of 5% or 10 knots (whichever is greater) from what's filed must be reported.

quiz.question: A report required only when NOT in radar contact:
choices: Position over each compulsory reporting point
quiz.explanation: Compulsory position reports (and ETA changes >3 min) apply in a non-radar environment; the others are always required.

lessons.title: IFR Equipment: GRABCARD + the Checks
lessons.hook: Is this airplane even legal for IFR? Grab a card.

quiz.question: In GRABCARD, the second A stands for:
quiz.explanation: G-R-A-B-C-A-R-D: Generator, Radios, Altimeter, Ball, Clock, Attitude indicator, Rate of turn, Directional gyro. (91.205(d))

quiz.question: The altimeter/static system (91.411) and transponder (91.413) checks are required every:
quiz.explanation: Both inspections run on a 24-calendar-month clock — and IFR flight requires the 91.411 check to be current.

quiz.question: The clock required for IFR must display:
choices: Hours, minutes, seconds — sweep hand or digital
quiz.explanation: 91.205(d) requires a clock showing hours, minutes, and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation.

lessons.title: DA vs MDA (and the 91.175 Big Three)
lessons.hook: One altitude you decide AT. One you park ON. Mix them up and the FAA writes.

quiz.question: The key operational difference: at an MDA you...
choices: Level off and maintain it until landing criteria or the missed point
Descend 100 ft lower to look for the runway
quiz.explanation: MDA is a floor you hold on a non-precision approach; DA is where you decide during a continuous guided descent.

quiz.question: Descending below DA or MDA requires (14 CFR 91.175(c)):
choices: Normal-landing position + required flight visibility + runway environment in sight
quiz.explanation: All three: continuous position for a normal descent/landing, the flight visibility on the plate, and a visual reference from the 91.175(c)(3) list.

quiz.question: Seeing ONLY the approach light system, you may descend below mins but no lower than:
choices: 100 ft above touchdown zone elevation (unless red terminating/side-row bars are visible)
You may not descend at all
quiz.explanation: 91.175(c)(3)(i): approach lights alone get you to 100 ft above TDZE — lower requires the red terminating or side-row bars, or another runway reference.

lessons.title: DPs & STARs: The On-Ramps and Off-Ramps
lessons.hook: The airway system has on-ramps and off-ramps. Here's how to merge.

quiz.question: The primary purpose of an ODP is:
quiz.explanation: ODPs exist solely for obstruction clearance and may be flown without an ATC clearance; SIDs add flow management and are assigned.

quiz.question: Unless otherwise published, an IFR departure procedure assumes a minimum climb of:
quiz.explanation: The standard is crossing the departure end at 35 ft and climbing 200 ft/NM — a gradient, not a rate. Convert using groundspeed.

quiz.question: Cleared to "descend via" a STAR, you should:
choices: Comply with the published altitude (and speed) restrictions on the chart
Descend to the lowest chart altitude immediately
Wait for a hard altitude from ATC
quiz.explanation: "Descend via" delegates the vertical profile to you — fly the STAR's published restrictions without further instruction.
